title: Always Take From the Biggest Pile
statement:
`gifts[i]` is the number of gifts in pile `i`. Every second you pick the pile with the **most** gifts (any one of them if there is a tie) and take away all but `floor(sqrt(pile))` gifts: the pile then holds `floor(sqrt(pile))` gifts (the square root rounded down).

After `k` seconds, return the **total number of gifts** left in all piles.

examples.explanation: 100 becomes 10, then 36 becomes 6, then 16 becomes 4: piles 6, 10, 4 are left: 20.
A pile of 1 stays 1, so nothing changes.

hints.nudge: After you shrink the biggest pile it may no longer be the biggest. How do you find the biggest pile again, quickly?
hints.pattern: A max-heap of the piles: pop the largest, push its square root (rounded down), repeat k times; the answer is the sum of what is left in the heap.
hints.pseudocode:
heap = max-heap of gifts
repeat k times: x = pop the largest; push floor(sqrt(x))
return the sum of the heap
hints.walkthrough: Searching all piles for the biggest in each of the k seconds costs O(n * k), which is fine for these limits, but a max-heap shows the standard tool: it gives the largest element in O(log n) and lets you put the shrunken pile back in O(log n). Do that k times and add up the remaining piles. A pile of 1 stays at 1 forever, so when the largest pile is 1 you could stop early. Take the integer square root carefully: floor(sqrt(10)) is 3.
